claims.text: Brittle behavior in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy emerges without conventional intermetallic precipitation.
Trace oxygen or nitrogen segregates to grain boundaries in the high-entropy alloy.
Impurity segregation produces localized solute depletion adjacent to grain boundaries.
Impurity-induced solute depletion causes a structural transition or loss of structural integrity at grain boundaries.
Impurity segregation and adjacent solute depletion reduce grain-boundary cohesive energy.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes embrittlement under stress and decreases overall toughness.
In a Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloy, trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during aging at 700°C.
Depletion of solute interstitials from the matrix during aging causes progressive softening in a Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloy.
Increasing oxygen or nitrogen content will lower fracture toughness relative to an impurity-minimized control.
Increasing oxygen or nitrogen content will cause earlier crack initiation under cyclic loading.
Impurity-doped and aged samples will exhibit altered grain-boundary chemistry relative to the baseline.
The impurity-minimized initial alloy has high toughness.
The impurity-minimized initial alloy has uniform grain-boundary chemistry.
The impurity-minimized initial alloy resists embrittlement under the proposed aging and cyclic-loading conditions.
The proposed comparison is restricted to conditions under which the alloy remains single-phase while being aged near 700°C and cyclically loaded.
The proposed mechanism may not explain brittleness after phase decomposition or gross microstructural coarsening.
The cited refractory-HEA evidence supports a qualitative link between impurity segregation and reduced grain-boundary cohesion.
The quantitative relationship between impurity concentration and toughness degradation is not established.
